title: Habit anchors
hook: B. J. Fogg's Tiny Habits: attach a new habit to an old one

segments.voice: Yesterday, when, then: a small practice tied to a moment that already happens. Did the moment come, and did the plan do the deciding? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

The toilet flushes. That's the moment. A Stanford researcher named B. J. Fogg has described doing a couple of push-ups right after, every time, because the flush was going to happen anyway. He doesn't mind the laugh. But it's a working example of a serious idea. Nobody has to remember to do the push-ups. The flush remembers for him. An old habit, one that never gets skipped, is carrying a new one on its back. Today's word is the name for that old habit: the thing a new practice can hold on to.
screen: `THE FLUSH IS THE MOMENT.` → `THE OLD HABIT REMEMBERS.` → `A NEW ONE RIDES ALONG.`

segments.voice: First, the anchor. In his book Tiny Habits, Fogg calls the existing routine an anchor: something you already do reliably, every day, without thinking. Brushing your teeth. Pouring the first coffee. Turning off the car. The anchor is solid, so it can hold weight. Second, the recipe. Fogg writes it as a sentence with two blanks: after I do this old thing, I will do this new thing. It's yesterday's when-then plan with a very particular kind of when: not a time on the clock, which is easy to miss, but an action that has already proven it happens. Third, the fit. Fogg advises matching the anchor to the new habit: the right place, the right moment, the right frequency. A practice of stillness fits better after setting down the keys than after starting the car. Fourth, an old pattern, with a twist on yesterday. Yesterday's psalm named times of day: evening, morning, noon. This text names actions instead. In Deuteronomy, the King James Bible says: "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." In Jewish tradition this passage is part of the Shema, said in the evening and in the morning. Sitting, walking, lying down, getting up: anchors that come around every single day. Fogg adds one modern touch: after the new habit, a small moment of celebration, a smile, a quiet yes, so the brain marks it as worth doing again. After this, that. And then a nod.
screen: `THE ANCHOR: WHAT YOU ALREADY DO.` · `AFTER I…, I WILL…` · `MATCH THE ANCHOR TO THE HABIT.` · then, large: `WHEN THOU LIEST DOWN, WHEN THOU RISEST UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: anchor one practice. Sit and settle on the breath. Now walk through an ordinary day and list its anchors, the things that happen no matter what: waking up, the first drink, leaving the house, coming home, brushing teeth at night. Pick the one that fits a moment of stillness best. Then fill in the sentence, silently: "After I…, I will…" Keep the second half small. Say it once more. Then let it go, and let the breath be the only thing happening. The bell holds the time.
Habit anchors. Things you already do every day, used as the hook for a new practice: after this, that. Today's word.
Your line: after this, that. Today, when your anchor comes around, do the small new thing right after it, and give yourself one small nod when it's done. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: People following B. J. Fogg's method attach a new habit to an existing routine with a short recipe, "after I do this, I will do that," and mark it with a small celebration; in Jewish tradition the Shema, which includes this passage, is said in the evening and the morning.

fork.setup: you want to add a minute of stillness to your day. which anchor do you pick?
options: after I set down my keys at home.
after I open my work email.
fork.reveal: Fogg's advice is to match the anchor to the habit. stillness fits a moment of arriving, not of starting to drive.

trapdoor: what you thought: a new habit needs its own reminder.
what it means: an old, reliable routine can carry a new one: after this, that.
what a scholar hears: Fogg's anchors are cues borrowed from habits already wired to their contexts; tying words to sitting, walking, lying down and rising is an old pattern in Deuteronomy.
